# Research notes: Acts 5:22–42

I ran out of search and fetch calls before I could cover everything, so some verses are missing and a few rest only on search snippets. I mark these as I go. There's a list of what's missing at the end.

---

## Traditional reading, verse by verse

**vv. 22–23 (the empty jail).** I only have Guzik's heading for vv. 21–23 and his note on v. 21. He says the apostles went to the most public place they could, the temple, as early as they could. While the leaders thought they were in prison, they were teaching God's word to ordinary people. (21-23) The apostles resume their work and are discovered to be missing from prison. i. They went to the most public place they could (the temple), and as soon as they could (early in the morning). When they were thought to be in the prison, they were obediently teaching God's word to the common people. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-5/

**v. 28 (the charge).** Guzik links the "strict orders" back to Acts 4:17–18, where Peter and John were told to stop teaching in Jesus' name. In Acts 4:19–20 they had openly said they would keep going in obedience to God. They had commanded Peter and John to no longer teach in the name of Jesus (Acts 4:17-18). Yet Peter and John openly told them that they would continue, in obedience to God (Acts 4:19-20). — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-5/

**v. 29 ("We must obey God rather than men")**
- **Guzik:** This was great boldness. The Sanhedrin cared more about what people thought than what God thought. The apostles weren't defending themselves or asking for mercy; they were simply explaining what they did. The New Testament generally teaches submission to authority, but submission to people is never absolute. This was a testimony of great boldness, in contrast to the Sanhedrin, who were more concerned about man's opinion than God's opinion. i. The apostles' response to the council was not a defense, nor was it a plea for mercy; it was a simple explanation of action. In general, the New Testament teaches that we should submit to those in authority over us. Yet submission on the human level is never absolute, and never is more important than submission to God. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-5/
- **Ellicott:** The same principle as Acts 4:19–20, but the angel's command in 5:20 now gave it new weight. The words are an assertion of the same general law of duty as that of Acts 4:19-20, but the command of the angel in Acts 5:20 had given them a new significance. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/5-29.htm
- **Gill:** Civil and religious rulers should be obeyed in anything that doesn't go against God's will. Where it does, God must be obeyed. men, civil magistrates, and ecclesiastical rulers, are to be obeyed in things which are not repugnant to the will of God; but in things that are, God is to be obeyed, and not men. — same page
- **Pulpit Commentary:** Calls this a golden rule for all people and all times. Peter doesn't deny he was given the order; he argues that God's command outweighs it. The rule is a golden one for all men, all circumstances, and all time (comp. Acts 4:19). Peter does not deny having received the prohibition, but pleads the superior force of the command of God — same page
- **Vincent:** The Greek word is stronger than "ought"; it means "must." We ought (δεῖ) Stronger, we must. — same page
- **Matthew Poole:** Compares Socrates, who told the Athenians he would obey God rather than them. as Socrates in his apology told the Athenians, I embrace and love you, O Athenians, and yet I will obey God rather than you. — same page
- **Constable:** This verse shows that apostles besides Peter and John had been arrested. Peter didn't try to defend their civil disobedience. This verse clarifies that the authorities had arrested other apostles besides Peter and John. Peter as spokesman for the apostles did not attempt to defend their civil disobedience but simply repeated their responsibility to obey God rather than men — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/5-29.html

**vv. 30–31 (hanged on a tree; Prince and Savior)**
- **Biblical Illustrator:** Every word sets what men did against what God did. They raised Him onto the tree; God raised Him to glory. Every word is chosen to mark the contrast between the act of men and the act of God. They raised Him up to the tree; God raised Him up to a glory that was the measure of His humiliation. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/5-32.html
- **Matthew Henry (Concise):** Christ gives repentance through His Spirit working with the word: waking the conscience, bringing sorrow for sin, and changing the heart and life. Christ gives repentance, by his Spirit working with the word, to awaken the conscience, to work sorrow for sin, and an effectual change in the heart and life. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/5-32.htm

**v. 32 (witnesses with the Spirit)**
- **Barnes:** The Spirit's coming, with its gifts and the conversion of so many, publicly proved the message true. The descent of the Holy Spirit to endow them with remarkable gifts Acts 2:1-4, to awaken and convert such a multitude Acts 2:41; Acts 4:4; Acts 5:14, was an unanswerable attestation of the truth of these doctrines — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/5-32.htm
- **Jamieson-Fausset-Brown:** The apostles witness as people who saw the facts; the Spirit confirms them through miracles. They as competent human witnesses to facts, and the Holy Ghost as attesting them by undeniable miracles. — same page
- **Bengel:** The Spirit's witness counts for more than the apostles'. The testimony of the Holy Spirit is weightier than that of the apostles. — same page
- **bible.org (Utley):** Pairing the Spirit with the apostles may reflect the Old Testament rule of two witnesses. Several times in Acts Peter referred to the fact that the Apostles and disciples are witnesses of Jesus' life and death and resurrection. In this context he adds, "the Holy Spirit" as witness. This may be a way of affirming the two necessary OT witnesses — https://bible.org/seriespage/acts-5

**vv. 34–35 (Gamaliel steps in)**
- **Chrysostom:** Gamaliel was Paul's teacher. Chrysostom notes how carefully he worded his speech and how he made the council afraid from the start. This Gamaliel was Paul's teacher. Observe how judiciously he frames his speech, and how he immediately at the very outset puts them in fear. — https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/210114.htm
- **Matthew Henry:** Gamaliel calls them "men of Israel" as a reminder: they should be guided by reason, and by God's revelation. He calls them men of Israel, to enforce this caution: "You are men, that should be governed by reason — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Act/Act_005.cfm

**v. 36 (Theudas)**
- **Chrysostom:** Gamaliel uses recent examples, not ancient history, because recent cases persuade best. "Before these days" means not long ago. does not recount ancient histories, although he might have done so, but more recent instances, which are most powerful to produce belief. With this view he throws out a hint himself, saying, For before these days Acts 5:36: meaning, not many days before. — https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/210114.htm
- **Barnes:** Josephus describes a Theudas under the governor Fadus, around AD 45–46. That was at least 10–15 years after Gamaliel's speech, so Barnes sees no reason to think they are the same event. Theudas was a common name, and two rebels could have had it. But there is no reason to suppose that there is reference to the same event — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/5-36.htm
- **Ellicott:** Josephus's Theudas had a "very great multitude," while Gamaliel says about 400. Josephus also says there were many uprisings after Herod the Great died. And it is hard to believe Luke would make such a mistake. — same page
- **Gill:** Some think Josephus got the date wrong. Others think this is a different Theudas; Origen placed him before Christ's birth. — same page
- **Calvin:** Admits that if we accept Josephus, Gamaliel's account departs from the true order of events. If we credit Josephus, Gamaliel altereth in this place the true course of the history. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/5-36.html
- **Coffman:** Argues the opposite: it is Josephus, not Luke, who is wrong here. it is not Luke but Josephus who is wrong in this instance, as in so many others. — same page
- **GotQuestions:** Treats them as two different men named Theudas. The Theudas that Gamaliel mentions is a different Theudas from the one appearing in Josephus' history — https://www.gotquestions.org/Theudas-in-the-Bible.html

**v. 37 (Judas the Galilean).** I found only one brief note. Meyer says that although "before these days" contrasts with ancient history, Gamaliel still reaches back to before the census of Quirinius. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/5-36.htm

**vv. 38–39 ("if it is from God")**
- **Guzik:** A warning that Gamaliel was giving his own opinion, not speaking for God. Gamaliel spoke for himself and not for God. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-5/
- **Matthew Henry:** Gamaliel's advice was to leave the matter to Providence and wait to see the outcome. "Wait the issue, and see what it will come to. If it be of men, it will come to nought of itself; if of God, it will stand, — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Act/Act_005.cfm
- **Matthew Henry (Concise):** The Lord still holds all hearts and sometimes uses the caution of worldly-wise people to hold back persecutors. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/5-36.htm
- **Origen:** Calls Gamaliel's remark very wise and uses it to argue that Christ, unlike the failed rebels, was truly the Son of God. — https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/04161.htm

**v. 40 (flogged and released).** The Bible Hub study note calls flogging a common punishment meant to stop further preaching. The apostles' departure signifies their release after being flogged, a common punishment intended to deter further preaching. — https://biblehub.com/study/acts/5-41.htm

**v. 41 (rejoicing)**
- **Benson:** As respected men, they would have felt the shame more than the pain of the whip. Still, they counted it an honour because it was for Christ's name. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/5-41.htm
- **Bengel:** "Counted worthy to suffer dishonour" is a deliberate paradox. He compares Philippians 1:29. — same page
- **Constable:** They didn't enjoy the beating, but they saw it as an honour. They did not enjoy the beating, but they considered it an honor to suffer dishonor for the sake of Jesus' name — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/5-41.html
- **NET Bible notes:** "Worthy" means considered worthy by God, and "the Name" is the name of Jesus. sn That is, considered worthy by God. — https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php?book=Act&chapter=5&theme=wiki&verse=41
- **Gill:** "The name" was often used in Jewish writings to mean God. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/5-41.htm

**v. 42 (teaching daily)**
- **Matthew Henry (Concise):** The apostles preached Christ, not themselves, and that was what offended the priests most. The apostles did not preach themselves, but Christ. This was the preaching that most offended the priests. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/5-36.htm
- **Kelly:** No human authority has the right to set aside the Lord's direct command. It is impossible that a human authority could be entitled to set aside the direct command of the Lord Jesus. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/5-41.html

---

## Where Protestant traditions differ

**v. 32 ("given to those who obey Him")** is the clearest split I found. Most of the tradition labels below come from StudyLight's own tags.
- **Reformed (Calvin):** "Those who obey" means those who believe in Christ. The Spirit is a seal showing God approves the gospel. In that they say to those which obey him, I refer it unto Christ, as if they should have said, those which believe in Christ are plentifully rewarded for their obedience. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/5-32.html
- **Adam Clarke:** The Spirit's gifts and graces grow in a person in proportion to how they obey the Spirit's first promptings. in proportion as a man who has received the first influences of it (for without this he cannot move in the spiritual life) is obedient to those influences, in the same proportion the gifts and graces — same page
- **Wesley:** StudyLight tags him Wesleyan/Methodist. His only note here is that the Spirit is "A much greater witness." — same page
- **Restoration Movement (Coffman):** God gives the Spirit after obedience, meaning after repentance and baptism (Acts 2:38). The Spirit is not given in order to make people obedient. there has never been any such thing as God's giving the Holy Spirit to men in order to make them obedient, or to make them sons, or to save them — same page
- **Dispensational (Constable; Chuck Smith, Calvary Chapel):** The obedience meant here is believing in Jesus. The Spirit indwells every believer. — same page
- **Don Stewart:** Rejects the view that the Spirit's power, or the Spirit himself, comes only to some obedient believers after conversion. He says Peter was talking to unbelievers about salvation. this passage has absolutely nothing to do with any reception of the Holy Spirit apart from salvation. — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/stewart_don/faq/baptism-with-the-holy-spirit/06-in-what-sense-is-the-holy-spirit-given-only-to-those-who-obey-god.cfm. Stewart describes the view he opposes, but I didn't find a Pentecostal source arguing for it.

**v. 29 (limits of obedience to rulers).** There is broad agreement here rather than a split, though the emphasis varies:
- **Calvin:** Stresses that when rulers and pastors act within their proper role, people can't claim "obey God" as an excuse to disobey them. Therefore, we must obey rulers so far, that the commandment of God be not broken. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/5-29.html
- **Geneva Bible notes:** We should obey man only in so far that in obeying him we also obey God. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/5-29.htm
- **Chuck Smith:** Lists Bible examples of refusing unjust orders (the Hebrew midwives, the three in the furnace, Daniel). — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/smith_chuck/SermonNotes_Act/Act_46.cfm

---

## Other views

**v. 36, modern critical view.** Thayer's lexicon (on Blue Letter Bible) says many hold there were two men named Theudas, but it considers it "far more probable" that Luke wrote an anachronism. others, with far greater probability, suppose that the mention of Theudas is ascribed to Gamaliel by an anachronism on the part of Luke. — https://www.blueletterbible.org/lexicon/g2333/nkjv/lxx/0-1/
- **ISBE (netbible.org):** Simply notes that Josephus dates his Theudas later (AD 44–45) than the speech (before AD 37). — https://classic.net.bible.org/dictionary.php?word=Theudas
- **Ellicott:** Reports that some critics take the error as proof the speech was made up years later. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/5-36.htm

**vv. 34–39, Catholic and early church tradition on Gamaliel.**
- **Catholic Encyclopedia:** Identifies him with Rabban Gamaliel the Elder of the Talmud. It reports an early church tradition that he became a Christian and stayed on the Sanhedrin to help believers secretly, and that Photius says he was baptized by Peter and John. At an early date, ecclesiastical tradition has supposed that Gamaliel embraced the Christian Faith, and remained a member of the Sanhedrin for the purpose of helping secretly his fellow-Christians — https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/06374b.htm
- **Clementine Recognitions:** Call him "secretly our brother in the faith." — https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/080401.htm
- **Chrysostom:** Says he cannot have stayed an unbeliever to the end. — https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/210114.htm
- These readings contrast with Guzik's warning that Gamaliel "spoke for himself and not for God."

---

## What I couldn't cover
- **Verses:** I found nothing specific on vv. 24–27 or v. 33. Notes on vv. 30–31 and 37 are thin.
- **Traditions:** I found no Lutheran, Orthodox (oca.org), catholic.com or bibleodyssey.org material, and no Pentecostal source of its own. Guzik (Calvary Chapel) is the nearest.
- **Popular teaching:** I found nothing on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace readings of this passage.
- **Fuller texts:** I couldn't read Guzik's full notes on vv. 34–42, because the page cut off and I only have search snippets, or the full Bible Hub pages for 5:31 and 5:37–40.
